flawed_step: The universal claim fails: semisymmetric graphs (regular, edge-transitive, not vertex-transitive) exist.
counterexample: Folkman graph. Vertex set: the 10 edges of K5 (side A) and two copies (u,1),(u,2) of each of the 5 vertices of K5 (side B). Join edge-vertex e={u,v} to (u,1),(u,2),(v,1),(v,2). Simple, 20 vertices, 40 edges, 4-regular (e has 4 neighbours; (u,i) lies in the 4 K5-edges containing u). Edge-transitive: S5 acts transitively on pairs (e,u) with u in e, and the swaps (u,1)<->(u,2) are automorphisms, so Aut is transitive on edges {e,(u,i)}. Not vertex-transitive: (u,1) and (u,2) have identical neighbourhoods (twins), while distinct edge-vertices {u,v} have distinct neighbourhoods {(u,*),(v,*)}, so no side-A vertex has a twin. Automorphisms preserve having a twin, so none maps (1,1) to {1,2}.
assessment_summary: Counterexample: the Folkman graph (doubled vertex-edge incidence graph of K5) is 4-regular and edge-transitive. It is not vertex-transitive because only one side of the bipartition has twin vertices.
